findings.claim: Roughly 125 million people lived under his rule, but only one in seven were ethnic Russians.
findings.truth: Great Russians were 44.31% of the empire in the 1897 census (55.7 million of 125.6 million). 'Fewer than half' is the safe form; one in seven is far too low.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Russian Empire Census' (1897 linguistic composition table)

findings.claim: examiners reward students who can characterise the writer's school of thought
findings.truth: Invented exam claim, and the opposite of the spec, which says the period-study interpretations 'do not require an understanding of historiography'. Rewritten around provenance and contextual knowledge.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, period study questions 1-3

findings.claim: Q 'What policy of forcing Russian language and Orthodoxy on minority peoples is known as ___?' A 'Russification.'
findings.truth: A fill-the-gap question with a one-word answer. Replaced with a substantive question and a fuller answer.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules

findings.claim: Critics inside the court called him 'the German' for borrowing capitalist methods.
findings.truth: Witte's father was of Baltic German descent and court reactionaries did attack him, but this nickname could not be verified in any source reached this session. Left as written; worth Tom's eye.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: By 1900 the Okhrana had infiltrated the Bolsheviks so deeply that ... Roman Malinovsky, was a paid agent
findings.truth: Anachronism twice over: the Bolshevik faction did not exist until 1903, and Malinovsky was recruited by the Okhrana around 1910, joining the Bolshevik central committee in 1912. Changed to 1914.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own text dates the Bolshevik split to 1903

findings.claim: By 1903 there were four main opposition currents: the Kadets (liberal, parliamentary), the Octobrists (conservative liberal) ...
findings.truth: Neither party existed in 1903. The Kadets were founded in October 1905 and the Octobrists in November 1905 - as the same lesson says two paragraphs earlier. Changed to 1905 in the panel and its revision tip.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own text

findings.claim: Nicholas wrote in his diary that constitutional government would be 'senseless dreams'.
findings.truth: The phrase comes from Nicholas II's address to a zemstvo deputation at the Winter Palace in January 1895, not from his diary.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Nicholas II of Russia' (statement to the zemstvo deputation)

findings.claim: Q 'Who founded the Socialist Revolutionaries in 1901?' A 'A merger of populist groups; the party drew on the older going to the people tradition.'
findings.truth: The answer names no founder, so it does not answer the question. Question changed to 'How was the Socialist Revolutionary Party formed in 1901?'
findings.evidence: internal mismatch

findings.claim: Examiners reward students who can distinguish between the different opposition groups ... a totalitarian-school historian (like Conquest) will read 1903 as ...
findings.truth: Invented exam claim plus historiography the spec says is not required. Rewritten to name the actual opposition groups and to use provenance.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1

findings.claim: Until 1917 the Mensheviks were generally larger than the Bolsheviks inside Russia.
findings.truth: Defensible for 1903-05 and for the soviets in early 1917, but the Bolsheviks had a delegate majority at the 1907 London congress and dominated the workers' curia by 1912-14. Overstated rather than wrong; left as written.
findings.evidence: contested; no single source settles it

findings.claim: The Treaty of Portsmouth in September brought home the Manchurian field army, who were used to crush the Moscow Uprising in December 1905
findings.truth: The Moscow Uprising (7-18 December 1905) was crushed by the Semyonovsky Guards Regiment sent by rail from St Petersburg on 15 December - which is what this lesson's own Moscow Uprising panel says. Ending the war did free troops generally; it did not send the Manchurian army to Moscow.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Moscow uprising of 1905'; the lesson's own collapsible

findings.claim: 'The Manchurian field army crushed the Moscow Uprising in December 1905 with artillery' and 'The Treaty of Portsmouth (Sept 1905) released the Manchurian army to be redeployed against the Moscow Uprising'
findings.truth: Same error as F11 repeated in two mark schemes; both corrected.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Moscow uprising of 1905'

findings.claim: A 'Artillery fire from troops returning from the Manchurian front.'
findings.truth: Same error as F11; answer changed to the Semyonovsky Guards sent from St Petersburg with field artillery.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Moscow uprising of 1905'

findings.claim: The St Petersburg Soviet of 1905 was the first
findings.truth: The first soviet was formed at Ivanovo-Voznesensk in May 1905. The lesson body is right ('the city's first soviet'); the definition is not. Changed to 'the most important of the first soviets'.
findings.evidence: standard account of the 1905 soviets; internal contradiction with the lesson body

findings.claim: By March 1906 the St Petersburg Soviet had been arrested, Trotsky among them.
findings.truth: The Soviet's deputies, Trotsky included, were arrested on 3 December 1905 - before the Moscow Uprising, not three months after it.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the 1905 revolution

findings.claim: Interpretation A is from Lenin's 1907 essay The Aim of the Proletarian Struggle, calling 1905 a 'dress rehearsal'
findings.truth: Anachronistic: in 1907 Lenin could not call 1905 a dress rehearsal for a revolution that had not happened, and the lesson body itself says he used the phrase 'later'. Replaced with a verified Lenin work that makes exactly the argument the question needs: 'Lessons of the Moscow Uprising', Proletary no. 2, 29 August 1906. The follow-up mark scheme was re-dated to match.
findings.evidence: marxists.org, Lenin, 'Lessons of the Moscow Uprising' (1906)

findings.claim: Bloody Sunday is dated 22 January 1905 (New Style) while the October Manifesto is dated 17 October 1905 (Old Style), neither labelled
findings.truth: Russia kept the Julian calendar until February 1918. Lessons 5, 6 and 7 label both calendars carefully; lesson 3 does not, so a student meets two 1905 dates on different calendars with no warning. Labelled rather than converted, in the unit's own house style.
findings.evidence: unit-internal inconsistency; lessons 5-7 as the model

findings.claim: Examiners frequently set interpretation questions on 1905 because it is the easiest period to misread.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten to keep the useful contrast without asserting what examiners do.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Lenin ... called it 'the awakening of Russia'; Nicholas told his mother he had signed it 'with sickness in my soul'
findings.truth: Neither quotation could be traced to a source this session. Both are plausible paraphrases of real reactions, so left as written, but they should be sourced or unquoted.
findings.evidence: no source found

findings.claim: The new electoral law gave one landlord vote the same weight as 543 peasant votes
findings.truth: The standard set of weightings for the law of 3 June 1907 is 1 landowner = 4 big bourgeois = 65 urban lower-middle = 260 peasants = 543 workers. The 543 figure belongs to workers, not peasants. I could not confirm this in any source reachable this session (WebSearch exhausted; Wikipedia's Duma and Coup of June 1907 pages omit the numbers, Britannica returned 403). RECOMMENDATION: change to 'the same weight as 260 peasant votes and 543 workers' votes' once Tom or a textbook confirms.
findings.evidence: unverified this session - Wikipedia 'State Duma (Russian Empire)' and 'Coup of June 1907' give no figures
findings.ruling: 1907 law: one landowner vote = 260 peasant votes = 543 workers' votes.

findings.claim: For interpretations of Stolypin, examiners reward students who can hold his repression and reform together
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. Rewritten as direct advice.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Nicholas abdicated, first for himself and then, after his brother refused the throne, for his son too
findings.truth: Sequence reversed. On 2 March 1917 Nicholas abdicated for himself and for his son Alexei together, passing the crown to his brother Michael; Michael refused it on 3 March, which is what ended the dynasty.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the February Revolution

findings.claim: Three centuries of Romanov rule had ended in five days / Within five days ... Nicholas had abdicated
findings.truth: 23 February to 2 March 1917 is eight days. Corrected in both places.
findings.evidence: arithmetic on the lesson's own dates

findings.claim: A week later, the second army was driven back at the Masurian Lakes.
findings.truth: The army encircled at Tannenberg was the Second Army (as this lesson's own flashcard says); the army pushed back at the Masurian Lakes was the First. 'The second army' invites the opposite conclusion, so changed to 'the other army'.
findings.evidence: internal contradiction with the lesson's own flashcard

findings.claim: Examiners specifically warn against eyewitness narrative voice ... it kills your AO2 marks
findings.truth: Invented exam claim and an invented mark consequence. The advice itself is sound and was kept without the false authority.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Nicholas dismissed his uncle Grand Duke Nikolai
findings.truth: Grand Duke Nikolai Nikolaevich was Nicholas II's first cousin once removed, not his uncle, though many British textbooks say uncle. Not mark-affecting; left as written.
findings.evidence: Romanov genealogy

findings.claim: Bolshevik party membership grew from about 24,000 in April 1917 to perhaps 350,000 by October (lesson 6 panel; repeated in lesson 7 body, flashcard and mark scheme)
findings.truth: 24,000 is the figure normally given for FEBRUARY 1917; by the April conference the party reported about 80,000. Wikipedia's Bolsheviks article gives 1905-07 figures only and the April conference page 404s, so I could not confirm either number this session. RECOMMENDATION: re-date 24,000 to February 1917 in all four places, leaving the October figure alone. Four locations, so a small ripple.
findings.evidence: unverified this session - Wikipedia 'Bolsheviks' carries no 1917 membership figures
findings.ruling: 24,000 re-dated to February 1917 wherever it appeared with April.

findings.claim: Trotsky ... returned to Petrograd from New York in May ... Now he formally joined the Bolsheviks
findings.truth: Trotsky arrived in May but worked with the Mezhraiontsy; he and his group joined the Bolshevik party at its Sixth Congress later that summer. Wikipedia dates his joining to August 1917.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Bolsheviks': Trotsky remained a non-factional social democrat 'until August 1917, when he joined Lenin and the Bolsheviks'

findings.claim: you cannot reach the AO2 analytical descriptors that way
findings.truth: Invented claim about mark descriptors, and descriptor language the house rules keep out of student copy. Advice kept, claim removed.
findings.evidence: house copyright-distancing rule

findings.claim: examiner reports flag the missing judgement step every series
findings.truth: Invented exam claim. The requirement for a judgement is real (the spec says question 6 is 'an essay requiring a judgement'), so the advice was kept and the false authority removed.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, question 6

findings.claim: Q 'Name the four most important White generals of the Civil War.' A 'Denikin (south), Kolchak (Siberia), Yudenich (Petrograd) and Wrangel (Crimea).'
findings.truth: A four-item list answer, which the flashcard rules forbid, and the lesson's match question already tests the same regions. Replaced with a single-focus card on Kolchak.
findings.evidence: house flashcard rules

findings.claim: Combined with civil-war disruption and the loss of Ukraine's grain belt under Brest-Litovsk, this triggered a catastrophic famine in the Volga region in 1921-22.
findings.truth: Brest-Litovsk was annulled in November 1918 and Ukraine was back under Soviet control by 1920, so it cannot be a cause of the 1921-22 famine. The cause the lesson omits is the severe drought of 1921, which is what the sentence now names.
findings.evidence: chronology given in the unit's own lesson 8 (treaty annulled eight months later)

findings.claim: Private trade was outlawed; the few who broke the rules were called 'bagmen' and shot.
findings.truth: Bagmen (meshochniki) were a mass phenomenon - an illegal food trade that kept the cities alive - and were normally arrested, not shot. 'The few' and 'and shot' are both wrong.
findings.evidence: standard account of War Communism

findings.claim: Examiner reports praise students who show consequences flowing into each other
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; advice kept as a direct instruction.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Lenin defended the NEP as a temporary retreat - 'one step backwards, two steps forward'
findings.truth: Lenin's 1904 pamphlet is 'One Step Forward, Two Steps Back', and it is about party organisation, not the NEP. The inverted phrase is widely repeated in textbooks as a NEP slogan but I could not source it. Left as written; worth Tom's eye.
findings.evidence: no source found for the NEP attribution

findings.claim: Trotsky published *Lessons of October* (1924)
findings.truth: Markdown asterisks do not render in HTML, so students see the literal characters. Changed to <em> tags.
findings.evidence: rendering defect

findings.claim: A 'November 1927, at the Fifteenth Party Congress.'
findings.truth: Trotsky and Zinoviev were expelled by the Central Committee in November 1927; the Fifteenth Party Congress did not meet until December 1927, when it confirmed the expulsions and expelled the rest.
findings.evidence: standard chronology of the United Opposition

findings.claim: name the school of thought to access top marks
findings.truth: Invented exam claim, and contrary to the spec's statement that the period-study interpretations do not require historiography.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, questions 1-3

findings.claim: Zinoviev as head of 'the Petrograd party' in 1924-26; 'They lost their Petrograd and Moscow bases'
findings.truth: Petrograd became Leningrad on 26 January 1924, five days after Lenin's death, so the 1925-26 events happened in Leningrad. Common shorthand, not mark-affecting; left as written.
findings.evidence: date of the renaming

findings.claim: As one historian put it, the dekulakisation campaign was less a war on rich peasants than ...
findings.truth: An unnamed 'one historian' is invented authority. The substance is sound, so the attribution was dropped and the claim made in the lesson's own voice.
findings.evidence: house rule on named interpretations

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag students who write 'collectivisation succeeded' without distinguishing ...
findings.truth: Invented exam claim, inside the lesson body rather than the exam tip. Advice kept, authority removed.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Examiner reports repeatedly flag the 'all kulaks were rich' misconception
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; advice kept.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: the Shakhty trial of 1928 that scapegoated mining engineers for the failures of the First Plan
findings.truth: The Shakhty trial ran from May to July 1928; the First Five Year Plan began in October 1928. It cannot have blamed engineers for failures that had not happened. It accused Donbas mining engineers of sabotage and set the pattern for the later wrecking trials.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own dating of the First Plan to 1928-32

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag this as the recurring weak point in answers.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside the lesson body.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: examiner reports praise students who name the metric they are weighing
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; advice kept.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Of the Red Army's eight marshals, five were shot.
findings.truth: The rank of Marshal of the Soviet Union was created in 1935 and given to five men: Voroshilov, Yegorov, Blyukher, Budyonny and Tukhachevsky. Three of the five were killed in the purges (Tukhachevsky 1937, Blyukher and Yegorov 1938); only Budyonny and Voroshilov survived.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Marshal of the Soviet Union'

findings.claim: Loss of experienced leadership: 5 of 8 marshals shot
findings.truth: Same error as F46 repeated in the mark scheme for the 8-mark question; corrected to 3 of the 5.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Marshal of the Soviet Union'

findings.claim: Trotsky was airbrushed out of pictures of Lenin's funeral
findings.truth: Trotsky was not at Lenin's funeral - the unit says so itself in lesson 10's mark scheme - so there was nothing to airbrush. The standard example is Lenin's speech in Sverdlov Square, Moscow, on 5 May 1920, from which Trotsky and Kamenev were removed.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Censorship of images in the Soviet Union'; internal contradiction with lesson 10

findings.claim: Yezhov himself was arrested in November 1938 and shot in 1940.
findings.truth: Yezhov was relieved of the NKVD post on 25 November 1938, arrested on 10 April 1939 and shot on 4 February 1940. The lesson merged the removal and the arrest.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Nikolai Yezhov'

findings.claim: *The Great Terror* (1968) and (*Origins of the Great Purges*, 1985)
findings.truth: Markdown asterisks render as literal characters. Changed to <em> tags. Both books and years are correct.
findings.evidence: rendering defect

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag students who write 'only old Bolsheviks were purged' - this is wrong and loses marks.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside the lesson body, with an invented mark consequence.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag the ... misconception ... this characterisation move is what top-band answers consistently do
findings.truth: Invented exam claim, plus advice to name historiographical schools that the spec explicitly says is not required.
findings.evidence: spec 4.4.1, questions 1-3

findings.claim: Stalin signed the German surrender on 9 May 1945
findings.truth: Stalin signed nothing. Germany's surrender was signed at Reims on 7 May and ratified in Berlin-Karlshorst late on 8 May, with Marshal Zhukov signing for the Soviet Union. It took effect at one minute past midnight Moscow time, which is why the Soviet holiday is 9 May.
findings.evidence: standard account of the German instrument of surrender

findings.claim: SMERSH (counter-intelligence under the NKVD)
findings.truth: The main SMERSH, created in April 1943, was military counter-intelligence under the People's Commissariat of Defence, answering to Stalin, not to the NKVD.
findings.evidence: standard account of SMERSH

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag the 'Stalin was always brilliant' misconception
findings.truth: Invented exam claim inside the lesson body.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

findings.claim: Examiner reports flag two recurring misconceptions on this period.
findings.truth: Invented exam claim; both warnings kept as direct advice.
findings.evidence: no such statement in the spec

summary: 14 lessons checked against the AQA spec, Paper 1 period study (six compulsory questions, 40 marks, 2 hours for the whole paper, no SPaG marks in this section). 56 findings: 6 HIGH, 44 MEDIUM, 6 LOW - 48 FIX, 6 NOTE, 2 ADJUDICATE - producing 64 edits across 13 lessons. The three biggest are the empire's ethnic composition (one in seven, actually 44%), the Red Army marshals (eight/five, actually five/three) and Stalin 'signing' the German surrender. Twelve invented examiner claims were removed, matching the count in the sibling Germany unit; four of them sat inside content_html, not the exam tip. The unit also carried a calendar inconsistency in lesson 3 (Bloody Sunday New Style, October Manifesto Old Style, neither labelled) which is now labelled the way lessons 5-7 already do. Question types and mark tariffs in the practice sets match the spec table and were not touched. No lesson is fully clean: lesson 6 carries only the ADJUDICATE on Bolshevik membership.
